Determinant and Permanent

VP ≠ VNPPermutationsAlgebra
Game: Arrange the digits 1 to 9 in the square to make one number, the permanent (or the determinant), as big as it can possibly be.
How to play: Click two digits to swap them. The list shows the six products that the numbers are made of.

    Look for the math

    This page starts a path towards one of the big open questions about computation, VP versus VNP. It is the algebraic cousin of P versus NP. At its heart are two polynomials that look almost the same: the determinant and the permanent.

    Same products, different signs

    Choose one entry from every row of a square, no two in the same column, like rooks that cannot take each other. Multiply them. A 3 × 3 square has 3! = 6 such products, and an n × n square has n!. The permanent simply adds them all. The determinant first gives each product a sign, + or −, according to whether its columns are an even or odd permutation. For the digits in order:

    det = 1(45 − 48) − 2(36 − 42) + 3(32 − 35) = 0
    perm = 1(45 + 48) + 2(36 + 42) + 3(32 + 35) = 450

    The best squares

    The logic test tried all 9! = 362,880 ways to place the digits. The largest permanent is 947 and the largest determinant is 412. The smallest permanent is 436, since every product is positive. A big permanent wants big digits multiplied together, so the 9, 8 and 7 should share one of the six products. A big determinant also needs the three minus products to stay small.

    Why the signs matter so much

    With n! terms, adding them up one by one is hopeless for large squares: 20! is about 2.4 × 1018. Yet the determinant can be found in about n³ steps, because the signs make it behave well when rows are combined. For the permanent nobody knows any way that is not exponential. The next pages show why.

    Can you find a square where the determinant is negative but the permanent is over 900?
